reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Classically presents with the triad of gait disturbance, cognitive impairment, and urinary incontinence, though not all three are always present
Gait difficulty is usually the earliest and most prominent feature and is often described as magnetic, broad-based and shuffling, sometimes termed a gait apraxia
It is one of the few potentially reversible causes of dementia, so recognition matters because shunting can help selected patients
Imaging shows ventricular enlargement out of proportion to cortical atrophy, and disproportionate widening of the Sylvian fissures relative to compressed high-convexity sulci is characteristic
Cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure is within the normal range, distinguishing it from obstructive high-pressure hydrocephalus
A high-volume lumbar puncture (tap test) or extended lumbar drainage that transiently improves gait helps predict a favourable response to shunting
Gait tends to respond best to shunting, cognition variably, and long-standing incontinence least reliably
The condition predominantly affects older adults and is frequently misattributed to ageing or Parkinson disease
reference.pathophysiology: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a communicating hydrocephalus in which impaired cerebrospinal fluid absorption leads to ventricular enlargement despite normal mean intracranial pressure. Intermittent pressure waves and altered periventricular compliance are thought to distort the corona radiata fibres, particularly those serving the legs and bladder, producing the characteristic clinical triad. It may be idiopathic or secondary to prior subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis, or head injury that scars the arachnoid granulations.
additionalDifferentials: Alzheimer disease and other neurodegenerative dementias
Cerebral small vessel disease with vascular cognitive impairment
Obstructive hydrocephalus from a mass lesion
Cervical or lumbar spondylotic myelopathy affecting gait
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain to assess ventricular size, callosal angle, and the DESH pattern of disproportionate CSF distribution
Large-volume lumbar puncture with pre- and post-tap gait assessment
Extended external lumbar drainage in equivocal cases to predict shunt responsiveness
Neuropsychological testing to characterise the cognitive profile
Assessment for comorbid neurodegenerative or vascular disease that may limit surgical benefit
redFlags: The full gait, cognitive and continence triad in an older adult should prompt evaluation for a treatable, potentially reversible cause rather than being dismissed as ageing
Rapidly progressive deterioration or focal deficits suggesting an obstructing mass or alternative diagnosis
Headache, vomiting or reduced consciousness indicating raised pressure and possible acute obstruction
Shunt malfunction or infection after surgery presenting with fever or acute neurological decline
reference.prognosis: Carefully selected patients, especially those with predominant early gait impairment and a positive tap or drainage test, often gain meaningful and sometimes durable benefit from ventriculoperitoneal shunting. Prognosis is worse when significant coexisting neurodegenerative or vascular disease is present or when symptoms are long-standing.
pitfalls: Attributing the syndrome to normal ageing or a primary dementia and missing a reversible cause
Selecting patients for shunting on imaging alone without supportive CSF drainage testing
Underestimating the surgical risks of shunting, including subdural collections, infection, and over- or under-drainage
Expecting equal improvement in all three symptoms when gait typically responds best and incontinence least
management: Offer ventriculoperitoneal shunting to carefully selected patients, especially those with predominant early gait impairment, as the definitive treatment
Select candidates with a large-volume lumbar puncture tap test or extended external lumbar drainage assessing gait response before committing to surgery
Use a programmable shunt valve and adjust it to manage overdrainage complications
Provide supportive gait and physiotherapy rehabilitation, continence management and cognitive support
Monitor after shunting for complications including subdural collections, infection and shunt malfunction
Assess for coexisting neurodegenerative or vascular disease that limits surgical benefit and informs prognosis
Manage jointly through neurology and neurosurgery
